utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84bis-PT. The Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj, Idriz Balaj and Lahi Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, good morning. Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. Paul Rogers, appearing on behalf of the Prosecution, together with Priya Gopalan, Ms. Barbara Goy, and our Case Manager today, Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Morning, Your Honour. Ben Emmerson, appearing on behalf of Mr. Haradinaj, together with Rodney Dixon, Andrew Strong, and Bath-Sheba Van den Berg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for Mr. Balaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour, Chad Mair, Colleen Rohan, Gregor Guy-Smith appearing on behalf of Mr. Balaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Morning, Your Honour, on behalf of Lahi Brahimaj, Richard Harvey, assisted by Sophie Rigney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Harvey. I'd like just to note for the record that according to the agreement reached at the last Status Conference on the 23rd of September, 2010, the accused are not in court today. Okay? Now, pursuant to Rule 65 bis (A) of the Rules, the purpose of the Status Conference is to one, organise exchanges between the parties so as to ensure an expeditious preparation for trial, and, two, to reveal the status of this case and to allow the accused to raise issues, including issues related to his mental and physical condition. Having this in mind, I'd like to recall that in the last Status Conference I issued the following orders: one, that the Prosecution should file by the 21st of October, 2010, a notification of the status of the two witness, Shefqet Kabashi and the other protected witness. Two, that all parties should file jointly by the 28th of October, 2010, a shortened form of the operative indictment corresponding to what is at issue in the partial retrial. Three, that the Prosecution should file its 65 ter list of witnesses and exhibits and its pre-trial brief by 30th November 2010. Four, that the parties should file a joint motion on agreed facts and issues by the 18th of November, 2010, and finally that the Defence teams should file their pre-trial brief by the 14th of December, 2010. I note that the Prosecution filed a notification of the status of the two witnesses Shefqet Kabashi and the other protected witness on the 22nd of October, 2010. The main purpose of this second Status Conference is therefore to discover what progress has been made in reaching agreements between the parties. The senior Legal Officer in Trial Chamber II has been copied on some e-mail exchanges between the parties concerning agreed facts. I have not seen those e-mails, but I understand the position to be as follows: that on the 1st of October 2010 the Prosecution sent a table of 32 proposed agreed facts to the Defence. That on the 22nd of October, 2010, each of the three Defence teams responded with their position on each of the facts, and that the intention was for the parties to meet at 9.30 this morning to discuss the matter further. I should now like to ask the parties where matters stand and what action they propose to take over the coming days to ensure that the order to file adjourned motion on agreed facts by the 18th of November is fulfilled. Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did meet at 9.30 this morning to have a brief conversation before coming into Court today. Your Honour, can I just correct one thing, if I may. The order for us to file on the 21st of October, the notification was complied with, and it was filed on the 21st of October. The notification we have is of receipt on the 21st of October. But the date that was given to it was the 22nd of October. But it was in 5.30 on the 21st, and I think according to the out-of-hours filings rules that counts as filing on the 21st of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So be it. You say it was dated -- the date given to it was the 22nd, the copy I have is 21st, sir. Then it seems to have the correct date. If you say it was filed on the 21st, then it was just a question of late filing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: It was. I didn't want Your Honours to think we did file late because we do try to meet our deadlines. In relation to where we head from here, we've had some very brief discussions but we plan to meet again after this Status Conference to further our discussions, and I hope that they will bear more fruit than has currently come on to the vine. We have received the Defence response to our proposed agreed facts. At the moment it's a fairly limited range of agreements. I expect we'll be able to eliminate the armed conflicts, and that's good because that will reduce the number of witnesses that need to be called, and, in fact, is a major components of any case in here. So that is -- it may seem limited, but, in fact, it is real progress. We just need to finalise the wording. And I think we'll also be able to eliminate some of the more technical evidence relating to forensics. There have been some proposals back to us, we can look at the precise wording, and I think we'll be able to reduce that. The more difficult areas, I think, will be relating to control and the position of the three accused. And that may be to some extent effected by how we propose to put the case. I think having spoken with my learned friends this morning, we can have some further fruitful discussion today which will help us to narrow the issues further, and it may well be that my learned friends will be proposing themselves some agreed facts relating more specifically to the judgement. Our position was taken from the indictment, we needed to start somewhere, and so we prosed matters that came from the indictment to see to what extent my learned friends would agree with that. Their approach, I think, and it's not unreasonable, is to go back to the judgement and propose effectively adjudicated facts from within the judgement. And I leave it for them to make any further explanation they wish to make about that, but, if they do propose those things, of course, we'll look at them and consider the extent to which we can reach that agreement having regard to those adjudicated facts. Of course, the difficulty with adjudicated facts is their rebuttable presumptions, and it might be that we want to rebut the presumption that was found in the trial that was not based upon the totality of the evidence we would put forward. But in short, I think we -- there is further discussion we can have today and I think it will prove to be fruitful, and I hope that we will be able to meet the 18th of November to at least define what is and is not an agreement for the purposes of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rogers. Just before I call the Haradinaj Defence team to stand up. Just two comments on what you've told us. The first two of the areas that you say you are still discussing on whether you can get agreement on, namely the armed conflict and the forensic stuff, we discussed this at the last Stats Conference and the expectation was that, in fact, those were the areas that you will deal with as a priority and most urgently. I'm surprised to hear that, in fact, they are still to be discussed and have not been discussed yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the wording that has come back from the Defence we can finish that today and relating to armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: There is a technical problem with the proposal arising from the judgement, and when one compares it with the judgement in Mos as to structure of the armed, but I think we can iron that out today, I'm confident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hope you will be able to iron that out. Let's hear what the Defence going to say. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I endorse Mr. Rogers' observation that we do not anticipate any difficulty in reaching agreement on matters such as the forensics which were, in any event, agreed in the original trial, or, indeed, in due course, on the armed conflict question. That simply will be a form of words issue. More controversially, one understands why the Prosecution did it this way, but the Prosecution's draft of the agreed facts essentially involves a recitation of broadly based allegations as they were put at the start of the last trial because they are drawn directly from the indictment on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't expect you to argue whether the facts proposed should or should not be agreed. I just want to find out whether you have agreed or you haven't agreed. I think you can argue with your learned friend outside of here to say, Look here, you are not going to present allegations to me, recite the indictment to me as a proposed agreed fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I was simply explaining to Your Honour how we end up here at this Status Conference without a full set of agreed facts. The short point, and I hope I'm reiterating what Mr. Rogers said to you, is that the Defence is approaching it from the point of view of those facts which were found after a trial. The Prosecution starting point being the allegations that they were making at the start of the trial, and obviously there is a need for some serious discussion and some work to be done between now and the 18th to ensure that what is placed before the Trial Chamber for the partial retrial accurately reflects the facts as found in the original trial. And I'm sure, in due course, there will be no difficulty in relation to that. Can I make one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I also make some observation on this point of adjudicated facts. We are finding ourself in a very unique position here in a retrial. For purposes of this retrial, how do the parties interpret the judgement of the Appeals Chamber on those issues that must come back here. If --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can they be said to have been adjudicated if the appeals Chamber says, No, no, no, I reject all this, go back and try the case again.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I interject that Your Honours anticipated precisely the rather general point that I was going to move on to immediately which is the architecture of the retrial in the light of the form of the Appeals Chamber's judgement. There's obviously two dimensions to the issues that fall to be tried in relation to the specific counts that will form the subject of the partial retrial. There is individual criminal responsibility, and there is an allegation of joint criminal enterprise relating to the KLA headquarters and alleged prison at Jablanica. And Your Honour will see and will have noted, and, indeed, recited the operative words of paragraph 50 of the Appeals Chamber judgement which was effectively to order a retrial on those counts in respect of the alleged participation of the accused in a joint criminal enterprise to commit crimes at the KLA headquarters and the prison in Jablanica. Now, that is a joint criminal enterprise of a very different scope to the joint criminal enterprise that was alleged in the original indictment, which was a, if I can use this expression, Dukajin region-wide alleged joint criminal enterprise. As a result of which the Prosecution alleged a very large number of individual crimes of which the Jablanica alleged crimes constitute a very small proportion. The Trial Chamber acquitted all three accused definitively and finally of both individual responsibility for all other crimes on the indictment and also for joint criminal responsibility through a JCE for all other crimes on the indictment, and by implication necessarily therefore for the existence of a joint criminal enterpriseDukajin-wide. Hence, the Appeals Chamber judgement confines, at paragraph 50, the scope of the retrial, which in our submission is to be conducted within the four corners of the language of paragraph 50 to a joint criminal enterprise to commit crimes at the KLA headquarters in Jablanica, those are the words used, that is the scope of retrial. So to that extent, all adjudicated facts that relate to any other form of criminal responsibility individual, direct, or joint are agreed facts, or, rather, adjudicated facts which stand and which were not appealed by the Prosecution. And there is no sense in which in our submission the Prosecution can be permitted, or, indeed, I hope would even attempt to use these small group of counts as a trojan horse, so to speak, through which to re-open questions of a broader joint criminal enterprise. Now, the reason I go into that short explanation at this stage is because it has implications, not solely for the agreed facts question, but also for the scope of the indictment which is to be filed by the 28th of October, and for a proper definition of the issues between the parties and therefore the scope of any evidence which may be relevant to those issues. Now, Your Honour indeed raised this issue at the last Status Conference indicating that Your Honour had your own view about what the scope of the retrial might be, although at this stage the Trial Chamber was not inclined to share that view with the parties without first, quite properly, hearing fully argued submissions on the point if indeed there remains a dispute. My sense, from a brief discussion with Mr. Rogers this morning, is that on reflection that is unlikely to be very much dispute, because the terms of paragraph 50 leave no room for misunderstanding and because there is a definitive acquittal of all three accused on all other counts and on the broader joint criminal enterprise. Therefore, Your Honour is quite right to say we are in a rather unique position because this is not simply a retrial but a partial retrial, and, indeed, a retrial of a very small part of what was a very large and broad-ranging indictment. Now practical implications are these: First of all, for the order that Your Honour has made that the parties jointly file a shortened indictment by the 28th of October. I'm going to invite Your Honour to vary that order simply to the extent of saying that the Prosecution should file an amended operative indictment. Because at the moment position is this: very kindly and as a matter of courtesy, the Prosecution has circulated to the Defence a proposed shortened amended indictment which effectively crosses out those individual allegations where acquittals have been returned and not appealed but leaves intact the very broadly expressed joint criminal enterprise, which the Prosecution failed to prove, and in respect of which acquittals the Prosecution mounted no appeal. That is obviously an untidy and potentially unsatisfactory situation where anyone to be under the miss apprehension that the indictment, as it would then stand, properly identified the issues for the retrial because it wouldn't, plainly the retrial would be confined to a much smaller allegation of joint criminal enterprise, namely that encompassed in the enabling order of the appeal Chamber at paragraph 50. So further work clearly has to be done on the indictment. But having made this point, both here in the Status Conference and directly in discussions into parties, which will continue after the hearing, I would respectfully submit that it is not for the Defence to frame the scope of the indictment. We may well wish, in due course, to take points on the way in which the indictment is framed. And we would not wish, therefore, to be in any way a party to the framing of the indictment beyond pointing out that the current proposal is plainly one which extends way beyond the proper scope of a retrial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I take the point that the framing of the indictment is the sole responsibility of the Prosecution, but that order was worded in that fashion precisely because of the fact that there was a need for the parties to have a common understanding of what is coming back for retrial.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would hate to have the Prosecution come here on a particular indictment and you coming and you just crossing over like that and not meeting because then you might not have had sufficient notice to what it is you are supposed to meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And to the extent that you are having discussions with the Prosecution on the scope of the indictment, to that extent are you making a contribution to what should go into the indictment, and it was with that spirit that the order was framed in those words.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think we are all very grateful for focusing the party's attention on the very issue that Your Honour raised at the last Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And let nobody be under any misapprehension, it is inevitable in the situation in which we find ourself that there will be some room for conflict between the parties as to what the scope of the retrial properly is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, it was quite clear in the first Status Conference that the positions of the parties was quite -- as to what should happen was absolutely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think -- I'm sorry to speak across, Your Honour, but I think as time progresses closer to the retrial, minds may become focused rather more clearly than they were at that stage, and what may have been rather unfocused thoughts are perhaps now taking rather firmer shape. And I hope that in the short submission that I've made, I've set out what is a very clear and I hope simple position that this is a case which is only before the Trial Chamber again by virtue of an order of the Appeal Chamber, which is encompassed in paragraph 50 of their judgement, the disposition. And it is only to the extent of that paragraph that any retrial can lawfully be conducted, and we would respectfully suggest, and I'm sure Mr. Rogers won't dissent from this, that the indictment and indeed the scope of his case as presented and any evidence he adduces must fall full square within that architecture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I judicially refrain from commenting on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Without saying any more about it, I think that will form the basis of the discussion that proceeded this morning. I anticipate we will have very considerable co-operation from the Prosecution and the Defence in that regard. But having said that, what, therefore, I would invite Your Honour to do is simply to amend the order so that it simply requires the Prosecution to file an amended indictment by the 28th of October so that the Defence are in a position to reserve their right, which they may well need to do during trial to take legal issue with any point arising on the indictment. I wouldn't want it to be thought that we in any way contributed to a document which we were subsequently to attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The order is so amended, if that's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm very grateful for that. Can I then move on to another point which Your Honours just raised, which relates -- rises, if I may say so, directly from the point that you made; namely, Your Honour is quite right to anticipate a risk that unless this issue is battened down pretty clearly, pretty quickly, the two parties are going to be anticipating a different scope of draft and that really has to be resolved, and we hope we will resolve it by agreement. But the fact of the matter is, the Defence do not at present know what the Prosecution intends to adduce as its case at trial. In other words, we don't know the case we have to meet. And at the moment, the only order that requires the Prosecution to enlighten us is the order that the Prosecution filed its final list of witnesses in pre-trial brief by the 30th of November. With the best will in the world, we very much hope that we will have a much clearer picture through co-operation between the parties and through the Prosecution, if I may say so, put it this way, laying its cards at least largely on the table before the 30th of November. But given that that is the outer limit date by which the Prosecution is required to nail its colours to the mast in respect to the point that Your Honour has raised, it does, with respect, seem to me on reflection that 14 days is too short a time to expect the Defence to respond. Ordinarily, of course, pre-trial briefs can be scheduled 14 days apart because the Defence will have had disclosure of the whole of the Prosecution case, so to speak, in advance and will therefore be in a position to anticipate what the case they have to meet is and then simply to amend what is already a very substantially drafted document in the light of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. But at the moment, unless Mr. Rogers is prepared to agree to an earlier date for a clear statement of his case, we are not going to know until the 30th of November how far, if at all, the Prosecution wants to adduce evidence going beyond Jablanica. And we would respectfully, therefore, invite Your Honour to extend by seven working days, the deadline for the submission of the Defence pre-trial brief. That seven working days, in facts, will take us to the beginning of UN holiday, and I was wondering in those circumstances whether - I know Mr. Rogers wouldn't object to this - Your Honour would consent to keeping the timetable as it stands other than that the Defence submit their pre-trial brief on the fist working day after the Christmas vacation which would be the 8th, I think, of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me make a few points. First of all, those dates were proffered by the parties themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And secondly, you referred to you don't know how far beyond Jablanica Mr. Rogers might want to go. At the last Status Conference, there were positions taken by the parties which I urged the parties to look at. The Defence anticipated that the Prosecution must call the two outstanding witnesses in addition to what is on the record in the previous case, and that was not the view of the Prosecution. And it was actually in the light of that that I asked the parties to make sure that they know exactly what they are coming for. If we go by what the Prosecution's position was at the time, we can expect or anticipate that if they are not only calling the two, there they are going to call more people to prove their case, to prove the six counts. I would, however, be surprised if they tried to proffer any evidence beyond the Jablanica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I would be surprised as well, but I don't know that the Prosecution has yet committed itself formally to that position. If Mr. Rogers is in a position to do that now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I suggest then that the deadline for the Defence be not tampered with at this stage, you receive what you are going to get from the Prosecution, and if you think from what you got from the Prosecution you will not be able to respond within 14 days, you can approach the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- and you can do so almost informally, seeing that we are still in the Status Conference -- in the pre-trial phase should you find that or by a very shortened motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm very grateful for that. I think that Your Honour appreciates the position of the Defence in relation to these matters and I think it's very clearly set out. I mean, if Mr. Rogers is in a position to give an indication this morning, obviously it will shorten things very considerably. Can I just raise one final matter. It's perhaps more in hope than expectation, but can I put it this way, is there any chance that we might persuade Your Honour to give us an indication as to the likely start date for the trial?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to start the trial as soon as possible in the new year.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well, thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: For some, reason, Mr. Guy-Smith, you are not coming through my ear. You are coming directly and being soft in tone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: How are we doing now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Much better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I don't want to go over those grounds that have already been discussed by Mr. Emmerson, but I do want to raise one structural point that I think is important for the Chamber's consideration, especially because of some of the comments that you've made. And I think the best example we have here is the issue of armed conflict which we all know is a chapeau requirement. It is our position that no party appeal the issue, that the Chamber, at the Trial Chamber level -- at the Appeals Chamber level, the matter was once again taken as being decided, and therefore this issue is no longer in dispute. It is, I suggest, the law of the case. And the reason that I'm saying that is because the use of the term and the use of the analysis of adjudicated facts does give rise precisely to what Mr. Rogers has suggested which is that they are rebuttable. As a matter of fact, in our situation which is a very unique situation, the reversal was based specifically on the six counts and was based specifically on a very discreet point, that point being the failure of the Prosecution to call those two specific witnesses. With regard to those facts that were found by the Trial Chamber, those facts were not disturbed by the Appeals Chamber in this reversal. And I would suggest to you, and I think that a starting point for building this case, is that we have a body of law which is the law of the case of this specific case upon which all parties can rely. It tightens the case, it focuses the case, and it leaves us in a position where we do not have to concern ourselves with re-litigating matters that neither party ever contested or disputed at the appellate point. I think that based on the conversations that we have had that we will be able to achieve relative agreement about most matters in the near future. But part of that once again deals with specifically whether or not the Prosecution is willing to limit themselves to the findings made in paragraph 50 of the Appeals Chamber indictment and the JCE that they have pled in this case. And at some level I think a part of what is occurring is that Mr. Rogers may well be putting the cart before the horse here because there is a JCE that has been pled and there are some specific crime-based counts that need be resolved. Nothing more, nothing less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to belabour issues that have already been well canvassed by my learned friends. I think we have already a strong basis for substantial agreement, the armed conflict issue is not going to contain anyone at all. Much of what the original Trial Chamber set out, particularly in paragraph 63 to 100 of the Trial Chamber judgement, will be something that forms the basis for, I think what Mr. Guy-Smith has put well, as being the law of the case and the facts of the case. So I think we are going to get close, and one of the great advantages often of holding a Status Conference is that it brings the parties together around the table outside the courtroom, perhaps even more effectively than it does inside the courtroom. And I think by the end of today, we'll be a lot closer to where Your Honour would like us to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Harvey. Mr. Rogers, do you have any reply specifically, for my purposes, to Mr. Guy-Smith's points of the law of the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, I do. Mr. Guy-Smith raised the question of adjudicated facts. What I was hoping we would be able to achieve is an agreement on a point or an agreement on an issue that doesn't revolve around adjudicated facts because they are rebuttable presumptions. And the last thing I wanted to happen was for us to proceed along an adjudicated facts basis on armed conflict and then to end up finding, having chosen not to call witnesses relating to that, that the parties seek then to relitigate the armed conflict by argument within the papers on the evidence that was available. Now, I note there are shakes of heads, and I'm delighted to see that there are shaking of heads and that that isn't going to happen, hence it seems to me sensible simply to just to agree the issue and then it's out of the way, and I, for one, remain comforted that that isn't going happen later on in the case. As to the law of the case, as I was listening, I just made a note to myself that there are at least two witnesses that were not heard, and the extent to which their evidence may impact upon the facts that were found by the prior Chamber, of course we don't know yet until we determine whether those two witnesses come again. So I'm hesitant on this notion of the law of the case because I'm not sure I entirely agree that the whole of the case has been settled when there are -- there's all -- and may be outstanding evidence or new evidence that we need to deal with. I understand my learned friends will argue with me, will take issue if I seek to go outside of the four square walls, as they put it, of the counts, and the four square walls of whatever the JCE is. And we may litigate that and argue about it, and the Court will rule. But at the moment, I don't fully accept that we do have a law of the case. However, I'm very content to receive any suggestions that my learned friends wish to make based upon that judgement relating to issues in the case concerning control command, that sort of thing, zone, geographical area, et cetera, et cetera. And we'll look at them and if we agree, Yup, we don't want to litigate that, we will agree it. That's how I see it. Could I just make one correction to the record. My learned friend Mr. Guy-Smith referred to it being a failure of the Prosecution to call two witnesses. I seem to recall that the Appeals Chamber judgement laid the criticism not at the door of the Prosecution when it reversed the acquittals. So that doesn't appear to be entirely accurate. Your Honour, my learned friend Mr. Emmerson asked me whether I'm prepared to commit to the Jablanica. At the moment I'm not, and he knows that I'm not prepared to do that today. But I'm very pleased that we will be able to have some constructive discussions. This is the first time I think we've been able to have a very focused discussion on what the scope of the indictment may be. Mr. Emmerson raised it with me this morning. I think it's the first time we've had that discussion, of course the first time he has been able to be here today. So I'm pleased that that has been raised, and I think we can take that on and move it forward. However, I do detect, perhaps I'm wrong, but I do detect a slight difference of emphasis between Mr. Emmerson and Mr. Guy-Smith perhaps, maybe I've misunderstood. But Mr. Guy-Smith's approach was that the JCE has been pled and all we are here to do deal with are the counts. I hear from Mr. Emmerson that he thinks that the JCE has not been pled which is why he is inviting us to look at the order of the Appeals Chamber and review the indictment to plead what he thinks the case is. And it would be very helpful if my learned friends at least were able to be consistent because I agree with Your Honour that it would be far better if we together, which is why I suggested a joint motion, could agree what the scope of this case is, rather than facing cross-litigation from my learned friends taking either point, you know, you don't amend the indictment, Mr. Emmerson takes a point; I do amend the indictment, Mr. Guy-Smith takes the point, and we end up litigating whether I should or shouldn't have amended the indictment. I hope we might clear that up between us.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I just in a sentence respond to that? There's certainly no tactical division of approach between myself and Mr. Guy-Smith. We obviously discussed what is a very difficult issue. Having said that, the very reason why I invited Your Honour to amend the order so that it would be the Prosecution's responsibility was in order to preserve the right of each individual accused to make such submissions as are properly open to them on advice as to the appropriateness and the lawfulness of the indictment as framed, and I certainly cannot undertake, and I am sure Mr. Guy-Smith and Mr. Harvey can't either, that we will necessarily give the same advice or received the same instructions, which is precisely why it is the Prosecution's job to frame the indictment. As matters currently stand, they have the indictment which extends far beyond the proper scope of the retrial. There may be, I don't know, arguments against them reframing a wholly different JCE, but equally there are arguments against them continuing in the trial where the JCE, as pled, goes very much more broad than the proper scope of the trial. And how that matter is to be resolved is a technical and difficult question, clearly the Appeals Chamber is of the view that there must be a retrial; therefore, there must be, in due course, an indictment. But it is not, I don't mean this rudely in any way but as I think is becoming perhaps even more apparent, it is not, should not, and cannot be the role of the Defence to contribute to the drafting of the indictment. It's Mr. Rogers' job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Emmerson. Let me say that once again I would like to strongly urge the parties to continue their discussions with the view to reaching agreements, if at all possible, so as to reduce the evidence that is to be adduced in the partial trial. Again I can pick up the positions of the various parties here. My understanding of the definition of the law of the case by Mr. Guy-Smith was slightly different from yours, and I would imagine that further discussions would clear you. You would be able to ask him what he means by that outside court, which you are not able to do here, maybe, or may not -- you could do it, but it may perhaps not be appropriate. So the Trial Chamber urges the parties please go ahead. And, yes, you did say, Mr. Rogers, that you wanted a joint motion on this point, but legally speaking, the indictment is responsibility of the Prosecution. So I would imagine that having had your discussions with the other parties and having agreed certain issues, the Prosecution will go and frame an indictment, hopefully in line with what has been agreed but taking sole responsibility for the indictment. If that would be a median position between the two positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. We, like my learned friends, have to look at the order that we've received and try to fathom it. And to that extent, I think there needs to be some understanding that we, too, are trying to comply with an order that the Court has made and that the Court ultimately must arbitrate on what the correct scope of this retrial is. So it may be that the Court will have to step in to any conflict that arises between us to determine what the correct scope of the order for retrial is. But let's carry on talking and it may be that we resolve some of those matters between ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure, indeed. And I hope you understand that the Court can only step in at the request of either or both parties, otherwise it will step in by way of judgement at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. We understand that. Obviously some Courts, of course, intervene proprio motu. But it appears that we would need to make applications in this particular Court, and it's helpful to have that indication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, unless there are other matters, there is one other matter I would like to raise with you, but I don't know whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Could we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Any other items, I am sorry, the parties would like to raise? Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I suppose there's no need to set a date for the next Status Conference. It will be set in due course as the need arises as we see progress, or would the parties prefer that we set a date?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we all understand that there ought to be another Status Conference before the end of this year, probably in December, and may we liaise between the parties and with the Chamber to identify a suitable date by which time we hope we'll be in a position to report back a rather greater degree of progress towards narrowing down the issues at trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Emmerson. While you are on your feet, you made a point earlier about responding in the first week of January or in the first week after the recess with respect to the Defence position.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Pre-trial brief. If we are having a Status Conference sometime in December, you don't think we need to have that after we have seen your pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, I think, if may say so -- Your Honour indicated that having seen the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, we would then be in a position to take views as to whether the issues were sufficiently narrowly defined. It's not even inconceivable that, as Mr. Rogers suggests, there might come a point where the Trial Chamber was required to give a ruling on the scope of the retrial. And having seen the Prosecution's pre-trial brief at the end of November, we will know whether that is the case, and there might even be scope, and we'll need to consider whether this is procedurally possible for that ruling to be given before the Defence responds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. In that event then we will not set a date, and as you rightly say, the parties will liaise and liaise with the senior Legal Officer. At this stage then if there are no other points to be raised. Mr. Harvey, you said you had nothing to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you also said so, Mr. Guy-Smith. Thank you so much. Well, the Status Conference stands adjourned. Court adjourned.
